tldr: This paper presents a whole-body control framework enabling a humanoid robot to pull a wheeled rickshaw with both hands, carrying loads or human passengers up to 115 kg—over three times its own body weight—with stable locomotion. It reveals an intriguing mechanical finding: by cleverly utilizing reaction forces from the wheels to damp lateral sway and roll, the robot actually expends less torque effort than when walking completely unloaded.

(a) The robot grips the handles with custom aluminum end-effectors and pulls a human passenger. (b) Relative spatial configuration between robot and vehicle. (c) While wheels bear the vertical load and constrain lateral slip, the robot provides propulsion and steering via the handles.
overview:
When making humanoid robots transport heavy objects, carrying or lifting them directly quickly hits physical walls: joint torque limits, structural strength bounds, and high tipping risks. This work takes inspiration from the traditional human "rickshaw." By offloading most of the vertical weight onto wheels while the robot focuses purely on forward propulsion and steering control, a humanoid should theoretically be able to transport massive payloads far exceeding its own body mass.

However, realizing this is far from simple. Because the robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact with the handles, the dynamics of its upper body and the vehicle become tightly coupled. Furthermore, in the real world, the passenger's weight, center of mass, wheel rolling resistance, and ground slope cannot be directly sensed. To overcome this, the authors built a three-stage training pipeline: first, a privileged teacher is trained in simulation with full access to vehicle states and contact forces; next, its actions and latent representations are distilled into a student network that relies only on on-board proprioceptive history; finally, the student is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning.

In hardware experiments using a Unitree G1 humanoid (weighing just under 35 kg), a single policy successfully handled starting, steady pulling, turning, and stopping without any payload-specific retuning. It towed payloads up to 115 kg (about 3.15 times its own body mass), including another robot and human passengers. Intriguingly, behavioral analysis revealed that the reaction forces transmitted through the handles act like a gait-synchronized damper, suppressing lateral sway. Across most tested speed and load conditions, the robot's joint torque-squared proxy was actually lower—meaning more energy-efficient—than walking unloaded.
contributions: Developed a whole-body control framework combining privileged teacher-student distillation and PPO fine-tuning, achieving robust tracking using only on-board sensor history without directly measuring disturbances or payload states.
Analyzed the behavioral and physical impacts of pulling wheeled loads on humanoid gait, showing that handle reaction forces provide a stabilizing damping effect on lateral and roll motions.

Demonstrated that pulling wheeled loads redistributes joint efforts, yielding a lower robot-normalized cost proxy (sum of squared torques) than unloaded walking across most tested speed and load conditions.

Deployed a single un-tuned policy onto hardware, successfully demonstrating real-world starting, turning, and stopping under diverse load conditions, including a 115 kg human passenger (approx. 3.15 times the robot's mass).

sections.heading: Why pull a rickshaw instead of carrying loads?
sections.summary: Carrying heavy payloads directly in human environments is severely constrained by joint torque and structural limits. Pulling a passive wheeled vehicle offloads vertical weight onto the wheels, freeing the robot to focus on propulsion and steering. This work aims to achieve whole-body locomotion that preserves stable balance and grasp under unknown, coupled load dynamics.
sections.details:
Humanoid robots deployed in human spaces are expected to transport cargo, tools, and even people. However, lifting or carrying heavy objects directly causes joint torques to spike and dramatically increases the risk of falling. Looking at the time-tested concept of a rickshaw, the wheels bear the vast majority of the payload weight. The robot only needs to provide propulsion and steering via its grip. Theoretically, this allows moving payloads far heavier than the robot itself.

From a control perspective, however, this creates a formidable coupled locomotion problem. The robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact on the handles, transmitting complex feedback forces stemming from payload mass, center-of-mass shifts, rolling resistance, and non-holonomic wheel constraints. Moreover, during real-world deployment, exact vehicle velocity, contact forces, and passenger weight cannot be directly measured.

Leveraging recent advances in reinforcement learning and privileged learning, this study introduces a controller that implicitly infers coupled dynamics solely from on-board proprioceptive history (joint positions, velocities, and IMU). Moving beyond simply pulling a cart, the authors also conduct in-depth behavioral and mechanical analyses to uncover the positive biomechanical impacts that wheeled load interactions have on humanoid gait and energy expenditure.

sections.heading: Evolution of history-based adaptation and whole-body loco-manipulation
sections.summary: This work stands at the intersection of history-conditioned locomotion adaptation and whole-body loco-manipulation. It builds upon prior studies interacting with passive wheeled systems, scaling up to dynamic, sustained two-handed pulling under unknown heavy-load dynamics.
sections.details:
### II-A History-Conditioned Locomotion Adaptation
Conditioning on temporal histories of observations and actions has become a standard approach for legged robots adapting to unknown terrains and disturbances. Paradigms like Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) train student encoders to infer latent representations of privileged environmental factors, while other works utilize Transformers to predict actions directly. This work builds upon the principle of implicitly estimating physical properties from proprioceptive temporal history.

### II-B Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Whole-body loco-manipulation integrates mobility with manipulation. Prior works have applied Model Predictive Control (MPC) with contact optimization, or reinforcement learning for pushing carts and moving boxes (such as WoCoCo and FALCON). While these laid the groundwork for contact force compensation and whole-body coordination, dynamic tasks involving persistent two-handed pulling of heavy wheeled payloads demand substantially greater physical adaptation.

### II-C Interaction with Passive Wheeled Systems
Passive wheeled objects, like carts and skateboards, introduce independent non-holonomic dynamics such as lateral wheel slip constraints. Although prior works like HAIC explored pushing and pulling carts, this study targets a rickshaw carrying human passengers—a system featuring massive inertia and unknown center-of-mass variations—and elucidates the underlying interaction mechanics through both simulation and hardware experiments.

sections.heading: Formulating rickshaw pulling as a partially observable Markov decision process
sections.summary: The coupled humanoid and two-wheeled rickshaw system is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The robot cannot directly observe vehicle states or external forces; it receives only its own joint and base sensor history alongside forward and turning velocity commands to govern its whole-body joints.
sections.details:
### III-A Robot and Rickshaw Hardware System
The platform uses a 29-DOF Unitree G1 humanoid. While equipped with Dex1-1 grippers, they lack the structural strength to pull heavy carts, so custom end-effectors machined from 6061 aluminum alloy were attached. Commercial rickshaws are too large for the G1, so a custom two-wheeled vehicle was built using bicycle wheels, a racing bucket seat, and aluminum framing (empty weight 22.8 kg).

The policy runs at 50 Hz, outputting target joint position offsets for all 29 degrees of freedom. A low-level PD controller tracks these setpoints while the grippers maintain a constant closing torque. The deployment observation vector $\bm{o}_t$ includes base angular velocity, projected gravity, joint positions and velocities, and previous actions, but contains zero information about vehicle velocity, contact forces, or passenger mass.

### III-B Task Commands and History Horizon
The commanded velocity $\bm{c}_t = [v_{r,t}^{\mathrm{cmd}}, \omega_{r,t}^{\mathrm{cmd}}]^\top$ specifies the rickshaw's forward speed and yaw rate in its local frame. Lateral velocity is omitted due to non-holonomic rolling constraints. The policy receives the current observation $\bm{o}_t$ along with a history of the past $H=61$ steps (roughly 1.2 seconds).

sections.heading: From privileged teacher to student: The three-stage training pipeline
sections.summary: Policies are trained through three stages: training a privileged teacher with full simulator access, distilling its latent states and actions into a student that relies solely on on-board sensor history, and fine-tuning with reinforcement learning to correct estimation drift. Carefully structured rewards enforce interaction stability and natural stepping.
sections.details:
### IV-A Privileged Teacher Policy Training (S0)
In simulation, ground-truth physical parameters are readily accessible: 7-dimensional static properties $p_{\mathrm{static}}$ (payload mass, center of mass, rolling resistance, ground friction, slope angle) and dynamic privileged history $p_{\mathrm{history}}$ ($61\text{ frames} \times 17\text{ dimensions}$, covering vehicle pitch, handle contact forces $\bm{F}_L, \bm{F}_R$, and relative kinematics). A causal dilated Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) processes these into a 12-dimensional privileged latent $\bm{z}^T_t$. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains the actor and critic.

### IV-B Student Network Distillation and Fine-Tuning (S1 & S2)
The student policy sees no privileged data and takes only its own proprioceptive observation history (61 steps). In **Stage 1 (Distillation)**, the teacher's action head is frozen and copied; only the student's TCN encoder is trained to mimic the teacher's latent representation and action outputs via supervised regression. However, latent estimation errors can still compound in deployment. Therefore, in **Stage 2 (RL Fine-Tuning)**, the action head is unfrozen, and both the student encoder and actor are fine-tuned end-to-end with PPO, allowing the policy to adapt to its own latent estimates.

### IV-C Coupled Reward Design
The reward function balances vehicle tracking, robot balance, handle grasp maintenance, and penalties on joint torque and action smoothness. To ensure natural gait, penalties are placed on foot-foot clearance violations, foot scuffing, swing-phase apex height deviations, and excessive ground impact forces.

### IV-D Domain Randomization and Training Environment
Simulations are performed in mjlab (MuJoCo-based) across 8,192 parallel environments on two NVIDIA H200 GPUs, taking about 11 hours. Broad domain randomizations cover vehicle mass (20 to 60 kg), center of mass location, rolling resistance, and terrain inclination (up to ~5.7 degrees).

captions.F3: Proposed three-stage learning framework. (A) Privileged teacher trained via PPO using ground-truth state and force information (S0). (B) Student distilled on proprioceptive history alone (S1) and fine-tuned end-to-end via PPO (S2). (C) Hardware deployment running at 50 Hz using only on-board sensors.

sections.heading: Pulling 115 kg on hardware! Why pulling is physically easier than walking unloaded
sections.summary: The proposed method achieved superior tracking and reduced oscillations compared to history-only baselines and fixed-arm control, generalizing well beyond training payload ranges. Biomechanical analysis revealed that handle reaction forces serve as lateral and roll dampers, reducing joint torque expenditure below that of unloaded walking under most conditions. Real-world tests confirmed successful pulling with a 115 kg passenger.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Tracking Performance and Ablation Studies
The proposed policy achieved high tracking accuracy, with forward velocity RMSE of 0.291 m/s and yaw rate RMSE of 0.0535 rad/s. Compared to an "Only History" baseline trained directly with RL, the proposed framework reduced vehicle pitch oscillations by 2.9%, yaw angular acceleration by 4.1%, and torso tilt by 4.9%. In a "Fixed Arm" baseline where arm targets were kept constant, tracking errors worsened by 52.3%, highlighting the necessity of active whole-body arm coordination.

### V-C Transport Cost and Joint Effort Redistribution
Evaluating Mechanical Cost of Transport (MCOT based on positive mechanical work) at 1.5 m/s revealed that quadrupling load mass from 30 kg to 120 kg increased MCOT by only 16.5%. Even more striking was the robot-normalized squared-torque proxy ($\mathrm{CoT}_{\mathrm{robot}}$): across almost all tested conditions—except extremely heavy 120 kg loads at speeds above 1.6 m/s—pulling the rickshaw required *less* joint torque effort than walking completely unloaded.
This stems from joint load redistribution: when pulling 70 kg, while knee squared torque increased by 126%, hip pitch torque decreased by 33% and ankle pitch torque dropped by 61%, yielding a net reduction in overall effort.

### V-D Gait-Synchronized Contact Coordination
Why does this occur? Analyzing handle forces throughout the gait cycle showed that the net lateral handle force $F_{\Sigma, y}$ is consistently in anti-phase with the robot's lateral center-of-mass velocity $v^C_{h, y}$ (correlation coefficient $\approx -0.91$). In other words, the rickshaw acts as a mechanical damper pushing back against lateral sway. Similarly, roll moments actively counter torso tilt, mechanically stabilizing the robot's gait.

### V-E Real-World Hardware Deployment and Sim-to-Real Alignment
The G1 humanoid was evaluated on hardware across three payload scenarios: 60 kg (carrying an empty G1 robot), 90 kg (small human passenger), and 115 kg (large human passenger, ~3.15 times robot weight). Using a single unmodified policy, the robot successfully executed starting, straight pulling up to 2.0 m/s, turning, and stopping. Joint velocity and torque RMS matched simulation trends closely, verifying robust Sim-to-Real transfer.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: Expanding tool-use capabilities in humanoids
sections.summary: This work successfully demonstrated heavy rickshaw pulling using privileged teacher-student learning conditioned on proprioceptive history. It revealed that coupling with wheeled loads stabilizes gait and lowers joint torque effort, enabling real-world pulling of over three times the robot's mass. Future work will target autonomous grasping, recovery, and uneven terrain navigation.
sections.details:
This paper presented a whole-body control framework for humanoids pulling wheeled loads, demonstrating that privileged distillation followed by RL fine-tuning yields high adaptability under unknown heavy payloads. The biomechanical discovery that contact with a passive wheeled system damps center-of-mass sway and reduces joint torque below unloaded walking highlights exciting new avenues for physical loco-manipulation.

Key areas for future improvement include removing the assumption that handles are pre-grasped by integrating autonomous visual detection, grasping, and regrasp recovery upon slippage. In addition, navigating uneven terrains and directly logging battery electrical consumption on hardware remain vital directions for future exploration.

takeaways: Pulling a passive wheeled cart rather than lifting loads directly is a highly practical strategy that multiplies a humanoid's payload capacity several times beyond its own body mass.

Persistent upper-body contact is not merely an external disturbance; when coordinated across the whole body, it acts as a mechanical damper suppressing lateral sway and roll while boosting energy efficiency.
For adapting to unknown load dynamics, distilling privileged teacher latents and actions into a history-conditioned student followed by end-to-end RL fine-tuning proves exceptionally effective.
limitations: Handles must be manually placed in the robot's hands before starting; autonomous approach, handle acquisition, and grasp recovery are not yet implemented.
Experiments were conducted predominantly on flat, paved indoor surfaces; navigation over obstacles, curbs, or rough terrain remains unverified.
Energy efficiency comparisons rely on simulated mechanical work and torque-squared proxies; direct electrical battery power measurements were not conducted on hardware.
